Researchers discover that simultaneous heatwaves and droughts have surged across Delhi since 2000, with future global warming set to slash the return time of severe twin-climate disasters down to just 14 months.
India’s bustling capital, home to over 20 million residents, faces a menacing climate double blow that is shifting from an occasional hazard to a near-annual reality. A new climate study by researchers from the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Bhopal and Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology (MANIT) Bhopal shows that Delhi is increasingly gripped by compound dry and hot events, which occur when abnormally high temperatures and severe rainfall deficits strike at the same time. The investigation shows that while these combined hazards were once rare and isolated occurrences, they have intensified dramatically since the turn of the century.
Compound dry and hot events are alarming because the atmosphere and the ground interact in a feedback loop. On ordinary hot days, moisture trapped within soils and vegetation evaporates into the sky, absorbing heat and providing a natural cooling effect, like sweating cools the human body. However, during a compound dry-hot event, an absence of rain leaves the soil parched. With no moisture left to evaporate, incoming solar energy directly bakes the dry ground, creating sensible heat that sends thermometers soaring higher and faster. In a concrete-heavy megacity like Delhi, this problem is aggravated by the urban heat-island effect, where paved roads and towering buildings absorb heat by day and radiate it back out through suffocating nights.
The research team examined high-resolution meteorological records spanning from 1958 to 2023 using the global TerraClimate database, which maps climatic variations down to a four-kilometre spatial scale. The scientists evaluated dryness using the Standardized Precipitation Index and thermal extremes using the Standardized Temperature Index. Rather than reviewing heat and rain in isolation, they merged both variables into a single mathematical measurement known as the Standardized Compound Event Index. They then tested these historical patterns against simulated future worlds warmed by two and four degrees Celsius using twenty cutting-edge global climate models from the international CMIP6 project.
The historical data revealed a turning point around the year 2000. Before that decade, extreme compound events were uncommon, with the most severe dry-hot combinations occurring only twice between 1958 and 1999. In the decades that followed, however, compound shocks clustered in rapid succession. The pre-monsoon months from March to June emerged as the most severely battered window, experiencing a massive surge in compound frequency and cumulative stress.
More worryingly, the warming simulations demonstrated that these twin extremes will no longer remain confined to early summer; they are expanding into the monsoon and post-monsoon months, steadily eroding the city's seasonal relief. The study shows that, if global temperatures climb by two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the most severe category of these compound crises could return almost twice as quickly as in the past. This translates to striking the metropolis roughly every fourteen months instead of every two and a half years.
By tracking both temperature spikes and monsoon droughts simultaneously at monthly resolution and introducing the concept of cumulative intensity across changing seasons, the study gives urban planners a timetable for how recurring climate stress accumulates over an entire year. As compound dry and hot events become routine, urban authorities can no longer manage heatwaves and droughts separately. By showing that these hazards arrive together, this study equips policymakers with the scientific justification to upgrade citywide emergency systems, expand rainwater harvesting, replenish over-pumped aquifers, and integrate passive cooling infrastructure like reflective roofs and green corridors.

Around 500,000 people from around the world are expected to participate in the 2027 Seoul World Youth Day, which will be attended by Pope Leo XIV.
The organizing committee held a press conference at Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul today (the 5th) to announce the preparation status for the event, which is scheduled to run from August 3 to August 8 next year.
World Youth Day is an event where Catholic youths from around the globe gather to interact, and this marks the first time it will be held in a non-Christian nation.
Pope Leo XIV is also scheduled to visit South Korea for the first time since his inauguration on the occasion of this event.
The organizing committee projected that 400,000 overseas pilgrims and 100,000 domestic participants will register, stating that approximately 81,000 people have registered from October 22 until yesterday.
The opening Mass, the Pope welcoming event, and the Stations of the Cross will take place at the Seoul World Cup Stadium, while the vigil and the closing sending-out Mass will be held at Seoul Air Base.
In particular, up to 1 million people, including unregistered participants, are expected to gather for the Pope welcoming event and the final day's sending-out Mass.
As large-scale outdoor events will continue in the mid-summer heat, preparations are necessary for heat-related illnesses caused by the scorching heat and for crowd crush accidents.
The organizing committee announced that it will prepare safety measures, such as setting up shade, water supply, and rest areas at the venue, and deploying emergency medical facilities equipped with cooling systems and professional medical staff.
In addition, they plan to operate a comprehensive response center jointly participated in by firefighters, police, medical institutions, and local governments to respond collectively to on-site situations.
For participants' accommodations, the goal is to secure space to accommodate 500,000 people by utilizing churches, home stays, school gymnasiums, and public facilities.

Meteorological officials forecast dropping night temperatures and gusty thunderstorms
Odisha residents should prepare for shifting weather conditions as forecasters predict imminent thunderstorms followed by a noticeable drop in night temperatures. Officials at the Meteorological Centre Bhubaneswar have issued a statewide yellow warning for isolated lightning and gusty surface winds reaching speeds up to 40 kilometers per hour for November 6. This alert covers all thirty districts, urging citizens to remain cautious during outdoor activities. These sudden weather shifts highlight the transitional climate phase typical for this region before winter fully sets in.
Night temperatures expected to drop
Forecasters indicate that while minimum temperatures will remain stable over the next 24 hours, a significant shift is on the horizon. Night temperatures across various districts will fall by two to four degrees Celsius during the subsequent three days. No large changes are expected after this initial plunge, signaling the gradual onset of winter chill across the state. Such temperature drops will bring crisp mornings and cooler evenings, especially in the interior and hilly terrains where residents will feel the cold more acutely.

Recent meteorological data reveals diverse weather patterns experienced across the state. Puri recorded the highest maximum temperature at 33.2 degrees Celsius, while Paralakhemundi registered the lowest minimum in the plains at 17.5 degrees Celsius. Daringbadi, a prominent hill station, reported a cool 17.0 degrees Celsius. Precipitation levels varied significantly across different regions during the preceding 24 hours. Mahanga in Cuttack district received the highest rainfall at 55.0 millimeters, closely followed by Jharbandh in Bargarh with 54.0 millimeters. Other notable rainfall amounts included Kujanga at 49.0 millimeters and Balikuda at 47.0 millimeters, both in Jagatsinghpur district. The capital city of Bhubaneswar experienced a maximum temperature of 31.8 degrees Celsius and a minimum of 22.9 degrees, along with minor rainfall of 3.6 millimeters. Meanwhile, Kataka (Cuttack) recorded 18.8 millimeters of rain with a slightly cooler night temperature of 20.6 degrees Celsius. State authorities continuously monitor the evolving weather patterns to ensure public safety.
